title: The Kingdom of God
lead: The Bible pictures God as King: over Israel from the exodus on, over all nations and all creation in the Psalms and the prophets, and, in the preaching of Jesus, as a reign that is coming near and will one day be complete.

sections.b: Israel sang of God as King long before it had a human king. The song at the sea ends, "The LORD will be king forever and ever" (Exodus 15:18), and when the people asked Samuel for a king, the LORD said they had rejected him as their king (1 Samuel 8:7). The Psalms make the cry "The LORD is King!" (YHWH malakh) the center of a group of hymns (Psalms 93; 95–99) that celebrate God's rule over the sea, the nations and the gods. Chronicles puts the same cry into the song sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:31).
sections.refs: Exodus 15:18; 1 Samuel 8:7; Psalm 93:1; Psalm 96:10; Psalm 97:1; Psalm 99:1; 1 Chronicles 16:31; Psalm 47:7–8

sections.h: The prophets and the coming reign
sections.b: The prophets look ahead to a day when God's kingship will be seen by all. A herald brings Zion the good news, "Your God is King!" (Isaiah 52:7); "the LORD will be king over all the earth" (Zechariah 14:9, a fresh rendering); and in Daniel the God of heaven sets up a kingdom that will never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14, 27). After the exile, with no king of David's line on the throne, these promises kept hope alive. In Jewish prayer, the Aleinu and the High Holy Day liturgy proclaim God as King and pray for the day his rule is acknowledged by all.
sections.refs: Isaiah 52:7; Zechariah 14:9; Daniel 2:44; Daniel 7:13–14; Daniel 7:27; Obadiah 21

sections.b: Jesus' first message in Mark is that "the kingdom of God has come near" (Mark 1:15, a fresh rendering), and Matthew usually says "kingdom of heaven," a Jewish way of avoiding God's name. Jesus taught his followers to pray "Your kingdom come" (Matthew 6:10). Christians differ on how far the kingdom is present now in Christ and the church and how far it waits for his return (Revelation 11:15). Many scholars speak of a kingdom "already" begun and "not yet" complete.
sections.refs: Mark 1:15; Matthew 4:17; Matthew 6:10; Luke 17:20–21; 1 Corinthians 15:24–28; Revelation 11:15
